newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelans don't understand labor reforms-Petkoff.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelans don't understand labor reforms-Petkoff.

text.p: Venezuela's Labor Law reform bill, heralded by both the government and the media as a historic breakthrough when passed by Congress last week, has sadly left most people in the fog, Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff said.

The bill, due to be signed into law by President Rafael Caldera later this week, has been called an historic breakthrough in Venezuelan labor relations, and was minutely covered during its uncertain passage through Congress by the local press.
But: "Unfortunately, I don't think most Venezuelans understand the new bill," Petkoff said during a television interview Monday, as part of a government drive to explain the new law.
"Then again, I don't think they understood the old system either," he added while taking phoned-in questions from perplexed midday viewers.

The bill tackles the complex and controversial reform of Venezuela's onerous and outdated severance/pension payment system, known as "prestaciones sociales" or literally "social borrowings", that Venezuelans view as a birthright.

Under the old system -- which government, unions and the private sector had unsuccessfully struggled to change in over 10 years of failed talks -- a retroactivity clause meant all previous allocations were calculated based on an employee's most recent wage.
That discouraged wages rises, especially during periods of high inflation, businessmen said.

Under the new system -- hammered out in mid-March in Tripartite talks -- workers will instead receive their severance payments annually based on their average salary for the year. The payment will be placed in a pension fund of the employee's choice.

That, says the government, lays the basis for Venezuela to move to a fully-funded social security system. Elimination of the retroactivity clause will also free up labor markets, private sector leaders have said.

"Hell, people want to know exactly where they stand (under the new reforms)," the plain-speaking Petkoff said after a straw poll revealed seven out of ten Venezuelans did not understand the implications of the new law.
